Mr. ORVIS A. KENNEDY (Edmonton East): Mr. Speaker, first on behalf of my party may I express regret at the sudden illness of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) which has caused him to leave the chamber at this time. It is our earnest hope that he will soon be able to return to his seat in the chamber.
It is with a feeling of regret and heavy responsibility that I rise on this occasion to deliver my first address in the house. I am reminded at what cost I take my seat in the house, the cost of the loss of a personal friend and gentleman in the constituency of Edmonton East. I refer to the passing last January of Doctor W. S. Hall.
In this address I propose to direct the attention of the house to some of the questions which were of vital importance to the
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy

Liberal-money reform. Even at this late date, three years later, it is again noticeable that money reform was not referred to in the speech from the throne and the budget. Surely it was not an idle boast; surely the Liberals were sincere when they made this promise to the people of Canada in 1935.
There is one other remarkable feature to which I should like to direct attention. The hon. Minister of National Defence claimed in Edmonton that the government had complete authority over the central bank; yet since that time it has been found necessary to purchase all the stock of this bank. Why is this necessary if they had complete control before? Let me quote again from the speech of the Minister of National Defence in Edmonton. After reading the preamble of the Bank of Canada Act, he said:
That is the finest charter of financial liberty you ever had. The government has complete authority and complete responsibility under the terms of that set-up. I suggest that all we need is a few more reformers from western Canada like Jim MacKinnon and Bob Marshall, and we will get action under that authority.
Tips is a plain admission, Mr. Speaker, that we were not getting action under the authority we had before. Now that the government has complete ownership of the Bank of Canada, all it needs is to control completely its policy and to institute a measure of monetary reform. This is advocated not only by all progressive parties in Canada but by some of the strongest supporters in the government's own party, and to emphasize this point I wish to quote from an editorial in the Edmonton Bulletin of June 1, 1938. This paper was one of the strongest supporters of the Liberal candidate in the by-election last March. The editorial says in part:
The Prime Minister has stated he will introduce legislation to completely nationalize the bank; a proceeding which would have no merit or purpose unless the bank is to be used as an instrument for the active administration of monetary policy for the purpose of creating and maintaining wholesome business and economic conditions.
The bank purchase decision implies repudiation of the idea that monetary conditions are shaped by the " times," and acceptance of the principle that money and credit can be so managed as to shape the " times." It is to be assumed the purchase legislation will be followed promptly by measures to employ the bank in this way; which measures parliament will have to either approve or upset the government and force an appeal to the country.
Parliament is therefore to be " put on the spot " on the subject of monetary reform. It is to be hoped the members will prove they were misjudged by Mr. Dunning and Mr. McGeer- and by a good many others-in assuming they had fallen into a stand-pat attitude on this issue-the one issue that offers them a chance to start the forces of rejuvenation and get the country out of the slump.

The Edmonton Bulletin has consistently stood for money reform, and I agree with it that money and credit can shape the times. The system must be made for man, not man for the system.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is the urge of many people in all parties that the government take immediate steps to introduce a ' definite policy of raising the standard of living of every Canadian citizen in keeping with the development of our natural resources. The people have consistently asked for security and freedom. They want taxation reduced; they want debts to be dealt with equitably so that they will be relieved from this crushing burden; they want poverty abolished. These are results that can be accomplished with an aggressive policy of money reform.
May I say just a brief word on unemployment. I do not wish to go into detail, so I shall simply state that since the government claim that it: is their right to control the purse-strings of this nation, they are the only ones who can introduce measures to alleviate the unemployment situation. Therefore the federal government should assume full and complete responsibility for the care of the unemployed.
In passing, may I say that as a young man myself I appreciate the efforts of the government in its youth training projects. I want however, to point out that you can train me or any other young man in Canada to be an expert in any line you choose, but if that young man has not a job he will not have the power to keep his home and family together round about him. Therefore the government must go one step further, and that is to occupationally establish our young people. I would also point out, while on the subject of youth training, that we have from Halifax to Vancouver one of the finest educational systems that could possibly be devised. We have efficient public schools, high schools, technical schools, colleges and universities- the best anywhere. The people of Canada -the fathers and mothers of our young people -by taxation are paying for these institutions, and yet we find that the only thing that is keeping their sons and daughters from attending these institutions, the only thing that is depriving them of the opportunity of an education in these institutions, for which their fathers and mothers are paying, is lack of purchasing power. Once again I suggest that this is an appropriate subject to be dealt with in the budget debate. I believe that we must change our obsolete economic system and modernize it to bring about the results for which the people of Canada are asking.

I should like to give, in some detail, figures in regard to the freight rate problem as it affects western Canada and particularly Alberta. It is a serious question with us, and you will find, Mr. Speaker, as I give the figures, that Alberta particularly has had a great handicap because of the freight rate situation.
It is a well-recognized principle in rate making that rates should not rise as rapidly as distance; this is the tapering principle. The average length of haul of commodities is much longer west of Port Arthur than east of Port Arthur. For example, in the case of grain the eastern haul is, on the average, 466 miles, while the western haul is 645 miles. Terminal and many other overhead charges are the same whether a ton moves 10 miles or
1,000	miles. Thus the longer the haul, the lower should the ton-mile rate be. That is, the overhead costs may be spread over a greater distance. Yet frequently we find that the western ton-mile rate is almost as high as or higher than in the east. For example, eastern grain moves an average of 466 miles and pays a rate of 60 cents per ton-mile, while western grain moves an average of 645 miles, or about 40 per cent more, and yet pays almost the same ton-mile rate. If the usual tapering principle were applied, the western rate would be 13-2 per cent lower than it is at present. Similarly, if the normal tapering principle were applied, lumber rates would be 31 per cent lower, and the rate on anthracite coal would be 52 per cent lower, and so on.

Wholesalers and jobbers, as well as the people of Alberta, suffer under this rate structure. This is a difference in favour of Vancouver of $0.73} per 100 pounds.
Flannelette blankets move to Vancouver in a cotton goods car at $1.75 per 100 pounds. The Edmonton rate is $4.53} per 100 pounds. This tremendous difference is principally due to the fact that the railways will not include cotton blankets in a cotton goods car to Edmonton. If these blankets could be included in a fourth class cotton goods car, the rate would be $2.33} and the discrimination would not be so great. The railways will accept these blankets in a fourth class car if the edges are not whipped. Unfortunately it is not practical to ship them in this shape, as the edges will fray. They cannot be shipped to Edmonton since no equipment is available. A rate structure that will allow a Vancouver wholesaler to bring blankets to Vancouver and reship local freight to Holden, a town sixty miles east of Edmonton, for 21} cents per 100 pounds less than is charged for shipment direct to Edmonton does not seem reasonable. The rates are $1.75 Montreal to Vancouver, plus $2.57 local freight Vancouver to Holden in Alberta, and the Montreal to Edmonton rate is $4.53}. The same discrimination in favour of Vancouver applies in the case of other dry goods, hardware, tools, and barbed wire.
At the other end of the prairie region Winnipeg is in a favoured position. In some cases Winnipeg distributors can ship l.c.l beyond Edmonton at a lower rate than the combination of the carload rate from Montreal to Edmonton plus the local rate. Many commodities can be shipped in car lots to Winnipeg and reshipped local freight into Edmonton territory at a lower total freight charge than would be the case if they were shipped direct in cars to Edmonton and distributed from there.
It is suggested that a substantial reduction in the rates on grain and grain products from Alberta producing points to British Columbia would do much to facilitate the interchange of commodities between the two provinces, giving each an increased purchasing power for the products of the other. These two provinces geographically are ideally situated side by side, each producing entirely different products which are required by the

other, but handicapped by a transportation cost between them which is relatively unfair to a federation of provinces.
To summarize briefly: Alberta, along with other western provinces, carries relatively a very large proportion of Canadian transportation cost, and in addition Alberta gets the shock both from the east and from the west. The old reasons of higher cost of construction and operation advanced by the board of railway commissioners for perpetuating this condition have been challenged from time to time. However, if Canada is to succeed as a nation, restraints of trade between the different portions must be removed, so that the products of the various parts may be freely interchanged, and if in the process the situation of the railways is too adversely affected, then the situation should be dealt with so that the burden shall be carried nationally and not disproportionately by various sections.
Another problem of vital interest to my constituency of Edmonton East is the coal situation. In or adjacent to the constituency of Edmonton East there are twenty-three mining companies in active operation, also the headquarters of many of the mines operating in the coal branches are in the city of Edmonton. One can readily realize how important a question this is to the people there.
However, rather than deal with any particular constituency I prefer to deal with the problem as it concerns Alberta as a whole. We all realize that the coal distribution is certainly far from satisfactory, and we would urge the government to look into the matter with a view to finding some means of making the distribution more equitable. Alberta alone has 14 per cent of the coal reserves of the world, 21 per cent of the coal reserves of the North American continent, 72 per cent of those of the British Empire, and 87 per cent of those of the Dominion of Canada. Yet we find the startling fact that, with all this coal in one province alone of Canada, Canada supplies only one per cent of the world's needs. Another startling fact we find is that, with all this coal, in 1936 exports decreased two per cent while imports increased 5-6 per cent. Upon a close examination of coal statistics in an effort to find where the difficulty lies, other startling facts are disclosed. Out of 28,000,000 tons of coal used last year in Canada, Canadian coal mines supplied only, in round figures, approximately 15,000,000 tons. Ontario brings in over 10,000,000 tons of coal from the United States of America. Surely a policy of Canadian goods in

The Budget-Mr. Veniot
Canadian homes, or Canadian coal in Canadian engines and stoves, would be the proper policy for this country.
The question is not one of production. We could produce far more coal in Alberta at very little greater cost than is the case to-day. When we examine the figures as to the unemployed -and I should have liked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) if he were present, to take particular notice of this fact -we find that last year we used a little over
5,000	miners underground in the mines of Alberta, but we have over 13,000 men holding miners' certificates. This means that approximately 8,000 miners were used in other industries, forcing other tradesmen on to unemployment, or that these miners were themselves being kept on relief. Another startling illustration is this, that the unemployed in Alberta in May totalled 8,771, approximately the same number that were kept out of work 'because we were not using coal from Alberta in Canadian homes.
Another clear illustration would be this. Ontario is sending about $100,000,000 into the United States each year to buy United States coal and bring it into this country. If we again compare figures, this is surprisingly close to the amount which the government at this time is trying to divert into a housing scheme in order to create employment. It is one case where money is going out which the government does not need to borrow in order to get; it is here, and it is being sent to the United States. If the government in some way or another could divert this flow of money amounting to about $100,000,000 from the United States into Canadian industry, this would do a great deal to stimulate employment in Canada. It is not that our coal is not as good as theirs. Alberta coal is every bit as good coal as one can buy anywhere in the world. The trouble is that we are not able to bring it to eastern Canada. I ask that the government check up on the question of subventions. We appreciate very much that the government are spending $2,-
250.000	in subventions in the Dominion of Canada, but we find that Alberta is getting only about $345,000. If we can get a larger subvention so that we can move Alberta coal to Ontario homes, this will stimulate business, I believe, all along the line.
Another suggestion which might be placed before the government is this. The order in council regarding subventions states that the subventions shall be provided by parliament year by year. If this grant could be stabilized in such a way that' it could be applied continuously, so that we could have it for a period of seven or even five years; or, in
other words, if the government could introduce a bill which would stabilize subventions to the coal industry for that period of time, we could interest coal miners in bringing the coal to the markets in Ontario. This would make it possible for the coal industry to establish warehouses at strategic points from which they could supply the Ontario market. This would have two advantages. It would make for greater employment, employment for men in these warehouses. It would also create the possibility of all-the-year-round work in Alberta mines and even in Canadian mines generally, to use a broader term. It would permit miners to mine in the slack season in the summer time and fill the warehouses, so that they would be prepared for the winter rush in the Ontario market, and would not crowd the domestic market in Alberta.
I am submitting these thoughts briefly to the government. I had hoped to take them up on the estimates of the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), but I am placing them on record in the budget debate so that he may look into them at this time.
Just to summarize what I have been saying in this speech: As a young man, I plead with the government to spare no effort in the interests of building a bigger and greater Canada. They have the means; we have the goods. I plead with them to spare no effort to build a bigger, better and saner Canada for the young people of future generations to live in.

speechtext:
I think it would be easier for the head of the department to give that explanation. The submission of the fishermen is that the present set-up of the Department of Fisheries is not in tune with the trend of the times when compared with the Department of Agriculture. It is not abreast of the developments which have taken place in the fishing industry in other countries.
During the past few years it has been my privilege to discuss with men who are deeply interested in the fate of the fishermen the various problems which confront them. Invariably the conclusion of these discussions has been practically the same, namely that the first and foremost step to bring the fisheries back to their former condition would be the uplifting of the fisherman and a complete revamping of the Department of Fisheries, so as to give it a set-up comparable with that of the Department of Agriculture. From a department of regulation, patrol and conservation there is an urgent need as rapidly and as completely as possible to transform it into a department of leadership, education, initiative, expansion and development in its relation to the several fields already mentioned, namely production, collection and storage; preparation and processing; distribution and marketing of fish. Let us briefly consider these few items.
First, let us consider the production and catch of fish. There is something radically wrong with fish-catch when people who live in the neighbourhood of the baie des Chaleurs and the gulf of St. Lawrence must both summer and winter send to Halifax wholesale fish dealers for their supply of fresh fish. There is something wrong when the fur raisers in the northern section of New Brunswick must every week import from neighbouring provinces tons upon tons of fish to be employed as food for fur-raising animals. Too many of our fishermen are still using the antiquated hand-line method of catching cod, and too great a number are without means of procuring modern fishing gear to increase their catch of other kinds of fish. The economics of this unnatural situation deserves study and consideration.
Second, let us consider the collection and storage of fish. This item needs greater attention. Here also the entire picture needs transformation under experienced leadership, just as has been the case in the Department of
The Budget-Mr. Veniot

Agriculture. Fish is one of the most perishable of protein foods. In order properly to preserve it in its fresh and edible state it is necessary, as soon as it is caught, that it be either processed immediately or subjected to some form of cold storage or freezing. Unfortunately a great number of our deep sea fishermen are not aware of this important fact and have not their boats equipped properly to store or to freeze their fish immediately, before it reaches shore. Only the large fish operators have boats equipped with these freezers or ice-boxes to take care of the fish in such a way as to render it suitable for further processing. The rest of our fishing fleet is obliged to subject its catch to some form of pickling, which renders it unfit for further delicate processing. In this condition steps should be taken either to provide some better system of collecting fish from the deep sea fishermen, or to give the fishermen the knowledge or facilities so that they may equip their boats to take care of their rapidly spoiling catch.
Third, let us consider the preparing and processing of fish. Leadership and education in cooperation with provincial governments, along lines similar to those adopted by the Department of Agriculture, are essential in the field of preparing and processing in new and attractive ways to make the product marketable and appetizing. Last year in my county a complete investigation of the fisheries situation was made, under the instruction of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud), and the one outstanding fact derived from the investigation was the lack of knowledge of the great number of fishermen as to methods of processing fish. Tons and tons of fresh fish could be filleted, smoked, canned or otherwise prepared if our fishermen only had the knowledge how to do so. The same applies no doubt to the majority of fishermen in many other sections of the maritime provinces. In this connection it might be fitting to point out that since 1934 the government of Quebec realizing the necessity of educating its fishermen along the lower end of the gulf of St. Lawrence and on the Gaspe coast as to modern methods of processing and handling fish, has officially established in that district a school to be devoted exclusively to fishermen so that they may be taught all a fisherman need to know about the preparation of fish and the methods of handling it when caught, and before it is brought to shore, so that it may reach its destination in as fresh condition as possible.
Fourth, I should like to discuss the distribution of fish. Valuable experiments have been

made by rail companies to discover the best methods of transmitting fish long distances for marketing purposes. But I suggest that one further step is important, namely the' establishment, at strategic points from coast to coast, of a chain of cold storage plants to' take care of adequate distribution. I do not imply that the government must construct and operate these cold storage plants, or go into the cold storage business. But we have here a need for leadership and initiative by a wide-awake and active Department of Fisheries which will create these distribution facilities.
The fifth point is that of marketing. It is hardly necessary to add that with a greater variety of fish products and with the creation of greater facilities for distribution and storage,, a much wider field of markets can be attained.. With proper leadership and direction there is-no reason why Canadian markets for fish could not be doubled or trebled. How many hon. members from the central provinces ever have on their tables fresh fillets of cod or haddock, fresh mackerel or herring, smelts, or lobsters, oysters or clams? In spite of the-present system of distribution one cannery in New Brunswick, which began operations on a small scale a few years ago, has succeeded in obtaining markets in over eighty countries. The individual small fisherman is not able-to enter such fields, unless some leadership is given by governing bodies.
Mr. Speaker, these are but a few considerations of facts as they exist in the fisheries industry. I leave them for the reflection of hon. members on all sides of the house, regardless of political affiliation. I feel sure they will conclude that there is plenty of room for improvement in the fishing industry. This appeal for leadership and for constructive action and development in connection with the fisheries is made in the interests of 200,000 Canadian citizens from the maritime provinces, coupled with several hundreds of thousands of citizens in other parts of Canada who depend for their livelihood upon this very leadership which they themselves have not the power or the means to develop.
They do not want charity. They are asking for light and guidance in their own field of endeavour, for an opportunity to develop their natural talents and to follow their blood tendencies to live off the sea. My submission is that in next year's budget the government should begin to make provision for the gradual but complete transformation of the Department of Fisheries from a department of regulation, control and conservation to one of leadership, initiative, education, action, expansion and development of the fisheries, patterned

The Budget-Mr. Taylor (Nanaimo)
on the development of the Department of Agriculture, as a first step towards rehabilitating what formerly was one of the richest industries in the maritime provinces, and in Canada as a whole.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise to my feet my good wishes go out to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) with the hope that he will speedily completely recover from the sudden indisposition which took him from the house this afternoon.
For a very few years, too few I regret, we have enjoyed the benefits of a general upward trend in business, but we have not yet been able to seal to ourselves the practice of balancing the budget of the country. We cannot be absolutely certain that business conditions will continue their desirable upward trend in the near future. Therefore, we must admit that there is no secure progress in our national affairs.
We face an utterly staggering situation. Our purely federal obligations stand to-day in excess of $3,500,000,000 gross, or $3,100,000,000 net. Before we can address ourselves to the necessary work of our country we must spend every year not less than an approximate sum of $117,000,000. Last year this amount stood at $134,500,000. This amount is needed purely for interest on money borrowed for work and services already done, sometimes overdone and sometimes demanding to be done again. Hon. members will not disagree with me when I venture to assert that to-day we are paying interest on capital debt the original reason for which has been lost to the country and its economy by the natural wastage of the years. Had I any inclination to pass out of the field of discussion of our national finances, I could bring to argument the story of many railways, many canals, many power plants and many industries and undertakings, the capital structures of which are staggering under items for the purchase of buildings and equipment destroyed or cast off many years ago, while the interest goes on year after year satisfying no one but the receiver, and in essence not even him.
Bear in mind that there has been no reduction in our national debt, nor can there be under the most promising of present-day conditions. There has been no reduction during the past eight years, and the continuing increase has brought us as a nation to an intolerable position. We have added a total of approximately $900,000,000 to our burden of public debt. In 1867, in the days of confederation. the public debt of the new Canada then being formed stood at approximately
$93,000,000. Seventy-two years have passed since that time, and during that period we have increased our debt fifty-seven times to a grand total of about $3,600,000,000. In that period we have only fifteen recorded years in which there was any reduction of debt. These reductions totalled slightly in excess of $319,000,000, leaving us with an addition to our confederation debt of about $3,300,000,000 gross, or $3,000,000,000 net. Do hon. members realize that there have been only fifteen profit making years in the seventy-two years since confederation? This means that in almost four years out of every five since that time we have complacently or compulsorily added to the debt structure of our country.
We do nothing at all about it. Reductions take place only when the budgeted accounts of the country disclose a satisfactory surplus. With that surplus the debts of the country are purchased and pro tanto reduced. But nothing is done to discover how we might whittle down our obligations and restore sanity to the economy of our people. It is not only in connection with the public debt of Canada that this has taken place. In every province and in every municipality the same obtains. We find the same condition existing in every country of the world where debts are privileged to accrete. Our debt is always increased by the surplus of our necessities, and the lean years eat up the depreciated revenue resources of our country. When the fat years come along they awake in us the urge to make up the leeway of our course, and we are quite satisfied to equate the growing needs of our growing country with the new financial resources of successful government. There can be little advantage in making of this speech a calamity howl, and I assure hon. members that such is not my intention. Still, I should complete the picture.
So far I have not considered the debts of the provincial governments which at the end of their 1936 fiscal years totalled over $1,700,000,000 for direct liabilities, less sinking funds. Neither have I considered the bonded indebtedness of the municipalities of all classes, which at the end of their 1934 fiscal years had reached the amazing total of $1,450,000,000, and these figures have since been climbing. What does it matter that these total exceed $6,250,000,000 net? Even then the tale is not told of the guarantees of interest, the guarantees of principal and such like. The thing which essentially matters is that we do nothing about it. The thing which eternally matters is that the wealthy men in our country know that they, more than wars
4150	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Taylor (Nanaimo)
and more than depressions, have produced this condition, but they are utterly helpless to bring sanity to its continuation.
It seems to be the accepted idea that a growing country can support a growing debt. While taxpayers protest and politicians grumble, never a voice is raised to declare that though everything else seems wrong there must be, there should be, there shall be a way out. Why should our public debt be considered as a snowball rolling down hill? Why should we complacently or in any other manner accept its growing size and assume that only when it reaches the valley of desolation will it melt? We have no justification for blaming the war or the war years for all our troubles? The war years numbered seven as far as this country's debts were concerned, but I have indicated a long series of fifty-seven years of unrelenting debits which were not all attributable to hard times. We are bound to admit that depression increases our public debt, while prosperity tends to give us confidence and encourages us in the enlargement of our public debt to meet our public needs. There is something very wrong with our economy and especially with our understanding of it. The facts I have marshalled are an advertisement of weakness which pleads for.immediate action.
The world has learned to accumulate and to develop wealth in the functioning of the capitalist economy, or, I should say, the neo-capitalist economy. The world very early and very quickly learned to demand interest on money lent. This is a highly important corollary of our neo-capitalist economy, and in spite of its generally blighting, parasitic nature, it is invariably protected and sustained by the full strength of our law structure.
We must therefore deal with it as we find it. We must also deal with the general economic situation as we find it; for these are the products of our brains, and in justice to ourselves and to those who will follow us. we must eliminate from both and from all our social machinery excesses and abuses which are constantly attaching to their functioning, human nature being just what it is. None the less it is no platitude to say that no effort of any kind, industrial, commercial or social, escapes the frustration which interest slowly but without surcease fastens upon it. Debts tend everywhere to increase. Interest tends everywhere to become more throttling, and I want to draw the earnest attention of the house, indeed of all the world about us, to this amazing fact, that there exists no machinery anywhere by which in our economy we can arrest their juggernaut
progress. The small cancellations afforded to successful citizens do not in historical survey provide any important solution of the situation, while the whole machinery of finance piles the interest of Pelion upon the debt of Ossa. There does not exist anywhere in the world to-day machinery to remove the pyramiding weight of both. Thus I assert that we move slowly and irresistibly to the collapse of our civilization without any intelligent effort being made to avert the catastrophe, and all this when we cry aloud for social security for our people and yearn for cultural opportunities for our spiritual development. In the present age we pay year by yeaT for the debts of the past, not in reduction of them, but in order that we may keep them alive for the honour and glory of, our good name and the dishonourable burdening of all those who may follow after us.
If I were asked, to tell hon. members what I think of interest, I would unhesitatingly classify it as a cancer upon the body politic. Long nights have I spent in concentrating on a way by which it could be painlessly extracted from our modern system. As I thought long and earnestly, I came to realize that in the end it might prove to be the goad to drive us out of the economic complacency in which we find ourselves, a complacency which permits us with unctuous pride to point to the unheard-of achievements of our modern civilization, while at our feet the drool of the cretin and the pathetic gaze of the helpless starveling scarcely move us to flick the crumbs from the tables of our gluttonous feasts.
For a very few moments, and before I move forward to any suggestion I desire to make, there is before me a problem corollary to my whole subject, to which I must refer. I refer to the present position of gold in the polity of any country. I have no illusions about the folly of building up huge reserves of gold. For many years I have predicted its ultimate elimination from the business of the world. It has been withdrawn from the pockets of the world, and it would be crazy folly for anyone to attempt to put it back. Its economic use to-day is to function as a make-weight in balancing international accounting, and I am quite prepared to admit that it will function in this way for many years to come, if happily the world does not completely fall to pieces in the meantime. At any rate I think we can agree together that its function internationally will be the last present power of which it will be deprived. It will be recalled that in the early

The Budget-Mr. Taylor (Nanaimo)
days of the great war the demand of Britain and her allies for food, equipment, and ammunition in unprecedented quantities created an alarming situation. Then it was that Sir George Paish took from the old country to Washington documents of security to a very considerable amount. These securities belonged to and had been collected from patriotic citizens, patriotic industries, and patriotic undertakings by the British government, and they represented investments of every possible kind which might prove acceptable to the government of the United States. They were lodged, shall I say, or deposited, or better still, hypothecated with that government, in order that a vast purchasing credit might be established in favour of Britain. It was to be a credit outside Britain, outside her normal commercial functionings-note that fact. This was done in the shortest possible space of time by British patriots. It was the first great historic effort of entrenched modern finance, by surrendering its forts, its guns, its immense stores of ammunition, to support in extremis the country of its patriotic owners and directors.
The release of these securities was not brought about until long after the war had ended, when Stanley Baldwin journeyed from London to Washington to acknowledge and commute the immense debt which had accumulated in the meantime.
Now our country, our Canada, is in extremis, tottering under a staggering load of debts, debts of capital, debts of interest, all borne by our little villages, our larger towns, our bigger cities, our provinces, and our Canadian selves. We must face these facts as they are to-day, and keen our brains, not our hearts, to discover a way out. Such a way out must not be lit by the flaming torches of revolution. It must not lead us into the cul-de-sac of renunciation, and surely as true Canadians it should not lead us into the wilderness of despair and frustration.
And facing the facts, Mr. Speaker, I say there is a way out, a way which passes by the very halls of finance, the very magazines of commerce, the very arenas of throbbing industry, and by the peaceful homes of our people. No unusual festival need mark our progress, and no unusual activity need herald our accomplishment.
If the wealthy patriots of Britain heard their country's call in 1914, then the wealthy patriots of Canada should hear their country's call to-day. They know how precarious is their hold on their so-called wealth. They know this more clearly than the millions of our people who have no such nether millstone
around their necks. They know that the last twenty years have witnessed no new avenues of great wealth open up. They have felt the pace during the past thirty years as it constantly quickened. They have felt the point of saturation slowly approach. They know that sooner or later, and better sooner than later, they must accept the call to face their responsibility and do their part, or be wiped off the slate forever in withering fatuity. Let them and their companies and their associations collect such gilt-edged securities as our scrutinizing government will accept. Have all the documents of title discharged in blank. Let them offer them to Canada absolutely free of incidental or other charges, under letters of deposit or hypothecation for a fixed period of not less than ten years.
At the expiry of that time they shall be absolutely freed by Canada and returned. Let Canada accept the condition that all accruing and developing interests and dividends proper to the securities shall flow to the patriot owners as usual during the term of the hypothecation. Let this be done to a first total of not less than $200,000,000 of acceptable and accepted securities, and I assert that the first great creative step will have been taken by Canada to lift herself out of the slough of despond.
This amount of $200,000,000 is well within the compass of the patriotic citizens of our country, and while large enough to make a distinct impression in the new plan is small enough not to disturb the safe and fluidic operation of the economic forces of our country. But there must be no strings to the hypothecation. The results of the working of the plan will be to the advantage of the wealth of the country and its holders to-day as to those who unequally bear its yoke.
Of course, it may be argued that this plan will involve inflation, and I therefore anticipate such an argument now before the plan is advanced. Managed inflation cannot be questioned. The country's first requirements in currency or otherwise were not scientifically arrived at; they were discovered accidentally and estimated arbitrarily and every variation since must necessarily fall into the class of inflation or deflation, theoretically at least. When we fail to balance our budget it is by a theoretically inflationary process that we cover, and when we develop a surplus we theoretically deflate to balance. This means that during the fifty-seven years since confederation when we failed to balance the budget the amount of the deficits were covered by the theoretically inflationary process.
