subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon his excellent expose of the country's financial affairs. It is indeed gratifying to see that a deficit of $77,000,000 has been reduced this year to approximately $13,000,000, and notwithstanding the predictions of the minister I hope next year will see the balancing of this country's budget.
The year 1937, Mr. Speaker, will go down in the history of this country as Canada's year. It was a year of substantial and definite progress in every field of productive activity; and notwithstanding difficulties both internal and external, the country made rapid strides along the road to prosperity. Agriculture, in spite of the drought which reduced the harvest in the west, on the whole was more profitable, and the buying power of those engaged in agriculture was increased. Mining development and production reached a new high level during the year. The wood industries were active, and it is gratifying to note that the value of the tourist traffic to this country rose to the figure of $200,000,000, very nearly equalling the 1929 record. The external trade of the dominion reached heights which had not been heard of for many years, and which compared favourably with the peak year in this country, 1929. Much of our industrial and trade activity was due in part to rearmament in Great Britain and also to the reciprocal arrangement made with the United States which, until the last months of 1937, operated strongly in our favour.
These rapid strides along the road to prosperity and recovery were rather suddenly arrested, and the picture to which I have referred was changed overnight, as it were. Suddenly we found ourselves in the midst of a recession. Gradually our trade with the United States began to fall off. Our neighbours, who had been buying from us in large quantities, ceased to purchase' the commodities which we were anxious to sell. The causes of this sudden cessation of purchasing are manifold. The fear of war; the accumulation of foreign capital in Canada and the United States; the disputes between capital and labour, and the concentration of wealth and power in the hands of a few, all contributed to the present situation. The recession in the United States began some time during the summer of 1937, and because of our intimate relations with our neighbour to the south, soon afterwards we began to feel the effects of that change. But let me say, sir, that this government took what I believe to be adequate and immediate steps to meet that oncoming recession. It at

The Budget-Mr. Chewier
once brought down legislation providing for a works program. It caused to be passed the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, by which $30,000,000 was made available to municipalities in this country for self-liquidating projects. It then brought forward for the consideration of this house the National Housing Act, which I believe will go a great distance in aiding this country towards recovery. This, sir, is truly a Liberal measure, and I believe it is by far the most important statute that has been brought down in this house by this or any other government looking to the solution of the problem of unemployment. By this measure municipalities, housing corporations and individuals will be able to borrow money in order to build low-cost homes. Then, in the budget resolutions, the minister removed the sales tax from building materials.
It is unfortunate that the proposed tripartite agreement between Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States should not have been completed in time to be included in the budget resolutions. It can be readily seen, however, that an agreement so far-reaching and so wide in effect could not be negotiated without a great deal of time and consideration. It is to be hoped, however, that the government will be able to conclude, these negotiations before the year is out.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer to another proposed agreement between Canada and the United States, having to do with the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway. The draft treaty, prepared at the instance of the United States government, was tabled in this house a short time ago. At this juncture, since the international commission has not been set up, I do not wish to declare myself either in favour of or against the proposal, but I should like to make a few brief observations in connection therewith.
The scheme of developing the St. Lawrence waterway is by no means a new one. As far back as I can remember it has been a topic of great interest in the community whence I come. Twenty-five years ago this question was debated and talked about a very great deal in and about the community of Corn-wrall. It was then said that some day the Long Sault rapids, which lie in the international rapids section, would be developed, and that they would generate electricity to such an extent that Cornwall and the surrounding country would, in time to come, be one of the greatest manufacturing centres in Canada. The hope was then expressed that we might have an entirely Canadian scheme, a scheme entirely within Canadian territory; and while that aspect is still possible so far
as the navigation end of the problem is concerned, it is quite impossible as far as the power aspect is concerned, because the power lies in the international rapids section, and that power cannot be developed without the consent of our United States neighbours. Engineers now affirm that it would be impracticable and unsound to canalize the St. Lawrence for navigation purposes only, and of course as I said a moment ago the power could not be developed unless we obtained the permission or consent of the United States of America.
The project, which at one time seemed to be a far-away dream, to-day is closer to realization than ever before. In my humble opinion, it is only a question of time before this scheme will be an accomplished fact, and when it is completed it will have the effect of making the area which lies around the lower end of the international rapids section one of the greatest industrial centres of this country.
The proposed new treaty would provide a two thousand mile channel linking the heart of the continent of North America at the head of the great lakes, to the Atlantic ocean. It would further provide a twenty-seven foot waterway from lake Superior to the sea. At present the channel is approximately twenty-two feet deep from the head of the lakes to Kingston, fourteen feet deep from Kingston to Montreal and thirty-five feet deep from Montreal to the sea. The international section, which extends from Cornwall to Kingston, is 115 miles long, and the whole of the scheme has practically been completed, save that part which lies in the international section.
The canals in the vicinity of Cornwall are only fourteen feet in depth, and those in the vicinity of Montreal are somewhat deeper. Towards the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway system this country has already spent $220,000,000, and of this amount over half, namely $131,000,000, has been spent in the development of the Welland ship canal at the Niagara peninsula. That canal is from twenty-two to twenty-five feet in depth. We have spent $23,000,000 in deepening the canals from Cornwall to Kingston, and $27,000,000 in deepening those from Cornwall to Montreal.
The other aspect of the project, which is by far the more important, namely the power development, is one which deserves consideration. The estimated potential power capacity of the whole scheme is 6,500,000 horse power, and of this amount 2,200,000 horse power lies in the international section. The United States is very anxious to develop its share of
The Budget-Mr. Chevrier

that power, namely 1,100,000 horse power, at Cornwall, and proposes that both countries enter into an agreement to canalize the St. Lawrence river and at the same time develop the power. The scheme of course offers many advantages, but one has to admit some disadvantages as well.
As I said at the outset, it would be folly for me or for any other member of the house to give an opinion upon the scheme before the international joint commission referred to in the treaty has been set up, and before that commission has given us details, first, with respect to the cost of the scheme so far as Canada is concerned and, second, with respect to the territorial and legal rights of this country in the project, and third with respect to the apportionment of work in the international section.
The draft treaty is far from clear as to the amount of money which will be spent for Canadian materials and as to the amount of work which would be given to Canadian workmen. It strikes me that great care will have to be taken that in the international section, where the works are to be carried on, even though they may be carried on in United States territory, Canadians should be given an equal chance with Americans to sell their products and to offer their labour. Otherwise there might be very great opposition to the scheme, from a Canadian standpoint.
So far as the treaty of 1932 is concerned, there is another point I would like to bring to the attention of the house, namely, that this treaty-and the plans so indicate-changes the location of the present canal and places it entirely within United States territory. That from an engineering standpoint is, I understand, to be the proper place in which it should be. However, I warn the international joint commission, when it is set up, that great care will have to be taken with reference to the location of this canal, because the canal has always been in Canadian territory. It has been used by Americans, and Canadians as well, in Canadian territory, and in my humble opinion it would be a serious matter to displace it unless some very sound reason existed therefor.
With the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway there is intimately connected the agricultural life of this country, because if the scheme is completed, unquestionably agriculture stands to benefit. There is, too, another element which enters into the picture, namely, the fact that the development of power will again bring into the urban centres large numbers of people from the farms. This country will have to decide whether it has not gone too far industrially, and whether 
it would not be better to assist municipalities to get their citizens or their ratepayers back on the farm, rather than to develop large blocks of power which will create new industries and bring large numbers of people from the country to urban centres. I leave this subject without saying more. I was anxious to make these observations which, I feel, are well taken, and which are perhaps premature. I was anxious to make them because this is a project of vast importance, and one which, were it to be completed, would affect the whole economic structure of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we are living in very difficult times. In the last quarter of a century many events have come to pass, and many phenomena have occurred. The turmoil of war, the fall of governments through revolutions, the advent of totalitarian states and dictatorships-all of these things have contributed towards the fall of the old order. These phenomena, unexpected as they were, have taken place in a very short period of time. Old boundaiy lines have been wiped out. Powerful dynasties have fallen, and empires have been divided up among nations. New governments have arisen, and new states have been set up. We in this country have not escaped the influence of these new ideas and new tendencies. And while we are many miles away from dictatorships and totalitarianism, we have within our country elements which would set up these forms of government.
The ability of democratic and parliamentary institutions to survive depends primarily upon whether or not economic depressions can be overcome within the limits of these institutions. Under dictatorships people will endure conditions which, if they existed under parliamentary or democratic institutions, would ensure the overthrow of such institutions in a very short time.
The year 1937 marked just twenty years since the advent of the first totalitarian state in Russia, through the October revolution. The most distinctive feature developed by that totalitarian state unquestionably has been the terror. This of course applies in part to the other totalitarian states, such as Germany and Italy. Terror is the only instrument sufficiently powerful to enable the attainment of the goal of totality. The best known feature of terrorism in Russia has been the periodic hearing of mass trials. Inevitably the crime with which the accused is charged is treason, and very often the form varies, from blowing up bridges to plotting military intervention. The evidence offered consists almost exclusively of the incriminating confessions of the accused.

The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
There has never been a case on record of a man failing to admit the crime with which he was accused. It is clear that the trials were never held for the purpose of deciding the guilt or innocence of prisoners. Clearly they were public demonstrations intended to create definite impressions upon the minds of the people. If there had been failure to increase coal production; if there had been severe food shortages; or, again, if peasant insurrections were about to take place, then a mass trial was likely to be staged. The first object of the mass trial was to strike fear into the hearts of all those who might be harbouring disloyal intentions; the second was to divert public opinion from public misfortune, and the third was to create the opinion that effective action had been taken to prevent the recurrence of the undesirable event or development.
The form of totalitarianism in Germany is very similar to that which exists in Russia. There is not a great deal of difference between bolshevism on the one hand and national socialism on the other. The tendency in Germany is to eradicate from the minds and hearts of the people the very essence of religion. Conditions in Italy are perhaps not as bad, but the dictator there possesses the same powers and he can make use of the terror if he wills.
I point to these conditions simply to show that while conditions in Canada may be difficult, they do not begin to compare with those that exist under totalitarian governments. The only way in which we can keep these new and false and untried ideas from our own country will be by a more equitable distribution of wealth, by bettering the conditions of the masses, of those who suffer and those who toil, and by bringing down legislation similar to that which was brought down in this house in the last month or so. By doing this, we shall prove to the Canadian people that peace, order and happiness can still be found within parliamentary and democratic institutions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate with a good deal of temerity, knowing as I do that I am speaking in the presence of many old parliamentarians who have been in this house for many years and who have served their constituents faithfully and well and have contributed much to the progress of the country. However, I shall try to be brief in my remarks. I have taken up very little of the time of the house, keeping in mind what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)
said during the first session of this parliament, that if members of the House of Commons studied their problems more and talked less we would make much better progress.
If each of the 245 members talked as often and as long as some do, this session would last not for four or five months but for four or five years.
There is nothing that has a greater effect on the life, prosperity and progress of Canada than the budget, and the present budget is no exception to the rule. I am sorry the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is not in his seat to-night, and I am sure it is the wish of every hon. member that he have a speedy recovery and be soon restored to health. I wish to congratulate him upon the clear and comprehensive manner in which he presented the budget. It has inspired us with new confidence and hope, and it showed us the great grasp he has of the economic problems that confront our country. However, one of the great hindrances to recovery is our immense public debt with its resulting tax burden that rests particularly heavily on our farmers and other primary producers.
My constituency of Lambton-Kent, formerly Lambton East, has the distinction of being one of the few counties or municipalities in this dominion with no debenture debt. Long ago we adopted the policy of balancing our budget and living within our income. If other municipalities had done the same, they would not be in the financial difficulties in which they find themselves to-day. As Canada is largely an agricultural country, the problems of the farmer are to our minds the most important questions before the Canadian people to-day. Their problems are important in more ways than one, considering the fact that nearly fifty per cent of the population of Canada reside either in rural parts or in small incorporated villages directly dependent upon the prosperity of the farmer. Thirty per cent of Canadian production is agricultural. It forms the basis of our export trade and is the lifeblood of our railways. In brief, the commercial and industrial existence of our country depends upon the primary producers. Unless the prosperity of the nation is reflected on the man who tills the soil, we cannot consider we have solved the problem of making Canada a land of prosperous, happy and contented people.
As long as the capitalistic system holds out; as long as the motive for doing business is the profit motive, we shall never be economically sound unless the profits of the primary producers are much greater than they are to-day. But I do not believe that we shall

The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
ever see a full measure of happiness in this or any other country until the great masses of the people receive a greater share of the wealth. I know the terror of the workingman's life. It is not so much the hourly wage; it is not so much the number of hours in a day that must be worked, the discouraging feature is the fact that a man has to live in constant uncertainty as to continuous employment. If the workingman were assured of fifty-two weeks of employment in every year, we would have a much more contented labour. Steady employment would give labour a greater buying power and thus provide a better home market.
That is all very good, but I am afraid we have the cart before the horse. Once a farmer is able to step into the buying market, much of our unemployment will take care of itself. We all know that the farmer is the greatest buyer we have of a large variety of goods. He needs manufactured goods in enormous quantities; he requires the services of hundreds of hired men and women, but he must have the necessary money or purchasing power. The removal of the sales tax on building materials will be of special significance to the farmer and will bring fresh hope to him. Any one who drives through our rural districts must be impressed with the need of farm building repairs. If there is any one in Canada who deserves a better home and modern improvements, it is the farmer.
I believe he will take advantage of this budget to the extent that his resources will permit. The removal of the tax on harness and harness parts will also help.
Unemployment insurance has little to offer to the producers in Canada's great natural industries, such as fisheries and agriculture, for they will be taxed along with the wage earners to provide the state's contribution to the unemployment fund. Minimum hours of labour are unlikely to be adopted by the farmers. With the high cost of manufactured goods and the comparatively low price he receives for his products, the farmer must work even longer hours. In 1920 a total of 110 bushels of wheat would buy a binder; at the present time it would take almost 400 bushels to purchase a similar machine. In order to produce this amount of wheat he would have to work, not eight hours a day, but eight hours in the forenoon and eight hours in the afternoon. Agriculture must be elevated to a place where the farmer will have faith and confidence in his calling as a means of livelihood. It seems to me that the people of this country are altogether too ready to forget the basic importance of this industry,

and the result is that the farmer is underpaid for his time and labour. We must remedy this by raising the scale of wages of those who work the land to a point in keeping with other classes, so that the rewards of capital invested in agriculture will compare favourably with the returns from other forms of investment.
I should like to say a word here for the sugar-beet farmers in my riding. These farmers have been growing sugar beets successfully since 1902, when the first factory was built at Wallaceburg. This industry produces around fifteen or twenty per cent of the total sugar consumed in Canada. The total acreage planted last year was around
50.000	acres with a total production of over
120,000,000 pounds of sugar valued at over $5,000,000. Almost thirty per cent of this acreage was taken care of by individual farmers and their families, and the rest was handled by contract labour. In the troublesome times during the last few years the farmer has been among the first to adjust himself to changed conditions, but the beet farmer has found it difficult to make things pay with sugar selling at $4.30 retail without the sales tax. The wholesale list price at Montreal is $3.90, and the refiners pay a field price of $5.50 per ton for beets. With normal prices and conditions this industry has possibilities. If Canada produced fifty per cent of her own consumption of sugar, we would require 20,000 workers, apart from office employees, and there would be distributed annually about $20,000,000. This would take care of many of our unemployed. I urge the government to help this industry by removing all or at least half the sales tax on beet sugar. The government tax of one cent per pound on sugar means a tax of approximately $30 per acre, which is much more than the farmer makes.
In this connection I might say that the economic life of this country is comparatively simple. Our primary industries produce, and the rest of us live by exchanging our goods and services for the products of the primary producer. I am not overlooking the importance of the home market, but we must not forget that in order to consume the wheat which we can produce in a normal year we would require a population of 30,000,000 or more people. The same might be said in regard to beef and hogs.
We have great natural resources, and I wonder if our immigration laws are not too strict. For the fiscal year ending last March our total immigration was 15,645. Of that number only 2,264 came from the British isles, 5,113 from the United States of America,

The Budget-Mr. McKenzie
and 4,464 from other parts of the world. Included in that number were 1,300 farmers and 339 of the labouring class.
In the southern part of my riding, where they specialize in certain types of farming such as the growing of sugar beets, tobacco, corn, onions and tomatoes, there is usually a distinct shortage of the right type of farm labour, and I would suggest that a selective ' and less restrictive immigration policy be adopted. This class of immigrant not only enhances farm values but actually creates more work, and they are consumers as well.
Walter C. Cain, deputy minister of lands and forests for Ontario, in answer to a query recently by the Rowell commission, reported that in northern Ontario there were approximately 6,000,000 acres of accessible land capable of agricultural development, but he did not see the likelihood of any rapid development taking place unless immigration bars were lowered. Consequently, if we doubled our population, our market problem would be easier.
I am not going to take up the time of the house regarding the great burden of debt, but it is interesting to note that in 1878, when Sir John A. Macdonald succeeded the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie as premier, the total expenditure of the federal government for all purposes was a little over $30,000,000 a year. Likewise, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in office in 1896, the total expenditure was $44,000,000. Now we are budgeting for an expenditure of over $500,000,000 a year.
In connection with government expenditures, I am informed that seventy-five per cent or the dominion's share of the old age pensions is $28,653,000, and the total cost under the Department of Pensions and National Health for the last fiscal year, including the cost of administration and hospitalization, is $55,570,945, or $11,000,000 more than the total expenditure for all purposes forty-three years ago. Mr. Speaker, these are stupendous figures, and the money must all come out of the taxpayers of this dominion. I am not finding fault with this expenditure but just wish to show some of our added costs.
My plea is that the government in all trade treaties and legislation should do everything possible to find markets, and profitable markets, for the primary products of Canada.
Next to that, cattle raising is probably the most important section of the agricultural industry in this country, and our system of marketing beef cattle is definitely bad. In the packing plants at Toronto and elsewhere there is little or no competition among the buyers, with the result that with a fairly large
supply of cattle the buyers set their own price and the farmers can take it or leave it. In this way the farmers are annually deprived of thousands of dollars to which they are justly entitled. I am advocating that parliament establish a select standing committee of this house to inquire into the cattle marketing problem, and to study ways and means of providing the British market with a steady supply of beef so that the producers will receive a square deal and the best prices obtainable.
We should not forget that the whole structure of our economic system rests upon the shoulders of those who till -the soil or otherwise begin the process of using the natural wealth of our primary industries for the benefit of humanity. Let us beware lest we place on the shoulders of those who support our economic life a burden beyond their ability to bear.
However, our recovery in Canada since 1929 far outruns -that of the United States. A chart recently published by the national industrial conference board of the United States, a non-political organization, and considered most reliable, shows that the downward trend from 1929 to 1933 almost paralleled the industrial decline in both countries, and the per capita debt of both countries was reduced by about five per cent; but since that period and to the end of 1937 industrial production has increased in Canada 4-8 per cent and declined in the United States 24-4 per cent. Employment in Canada, exclusive of agriculture, has increased 5'2 per cent but in the United States is down 6 per cent. While Canada's per capita debt has increased 22 per cent, that of the United States has increased 102 per cent, so that we are in much better shape than our neighbours to the south.
The government's decision to -take over the Bank of Canada is meeting with general approval throughout the dominion. This step will undoubtedly strengthen parliament's control of national credit. The need of some reform of our present monetary system is apparent to many, and though many theories as to how this can best be brought about are in evidence to-day, it is certain that we cannot continue borrowing money to pay our debts and that a halt must be called in that direction.
Trade negotiations between the British Commonwealth of Nations and the United States are meeting with many difficulties, but we are in hopes that they will be successfully completed at an early date. The general feeling is that trade treaties of this type are greatly to be desired at this time, so that
The Budget-Mr. Leclerc

we may develop a united front against the inroads of economic nationalism; and, of course, reciprocal trade pacts are fair to all parties and are conducive to prosperity and increased foreign trade alike. However, the success of such agreements is dependent upon the closest cooperation of government, producers, and business organizations in general.
Surrounded as we are by dictatorships, our only hope is in cherishing democratic ideals; and now these principles seem to be confined to the English-speaking peoples. Our first duty is to the bulwark of democracy, the British Empire. In Canada, the forces for disintegration are stronger than they have been for fifty years, with a possibility of the country breaking up into a number of sovereign states. Until this tendency is arrested and until Canada can achieve the solidarity at which confederation aimed, we cannot hope for national prosperity and progress.
Let me conclude by saying that if Canada is to continue to make progress, it must be as a united nation.	We Canadians have the
greatest heritage in the world, and we must think in terms, not of what is in the best interests of this section or that section, but of what is in the best interests of Canada as a whole-and not only nationally, but internationally. So I call on my fellow members to forget party politics and work together in order that this most desired goal may be attained.
Mr. JOSEPH H. LECLERC (Shefford) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, as I am rising to address this house for the first time since I was elected, permit me to offer the remark that I now better understand the meaning of the word parliament as applied to this legislative assembly. No other term could so well convey to the people of this country that an enormous quantity of idle words are spoken in this chamber, contrary to the custom of commercial, financial and industrial establishments, which are none the worse for that, seeing that they provide the government with its major sources of revenue.
Mr. Speaker, permit me to say further that, had I the parliamentary experience essential to preside over the deliberations of this house, I would not accept that honour without securing reforms which would enable me to apply closure to the saviours of the country who would make each session last more than twelve months a year, if every hon. member were to abuse his privileges as much as they do. I dare say, Mr. Speaker, that the government bills would not be less effective were they passed more rapidly, so that sessions could be shortened by half, thus saving several hundred thousands of dollars of the public funds.

My remarks are not in the nature of criticisms against those representatives of the people who, without abusing their privileges, state the legitimate claims of their constituents. I am now in a better position to appreciate the heavy burden resting on the shoulders of statesmen, and I cannot entertain any doubt regarding the devotion to duty and the sincerity of purpose of the majority of the distinguished public men who, in turn, assume power in our country.
Owing to its geographical situation, and to the diversity of interests of the different provinces from one ocean to the other, Canada is perhaps one of the most difficult countries to govern. We have not only the fishermen's problems on the Atlantic coast and the miners' problems in the Yukon territory, but also the intermediate problems of the different provinces. Some of them are industrialized and they want a legitimate protection for their industries so that they may be in a position to pay reasonable wages to workers whose health is rapidly declining in plants so extremely mechanized. The agricultural provinces of western Canada, having but few industries, advocate the lowering or the abolition of protective tariffs.
I realize, sir, what tact, what judgment and what experience are necessary to conciliate those divergent interests and consolidate national unity.
I have not the least idea of criticizing those hon. members who put all their talent to the service of the people whom they represent in this house. We see, for instance, members from the Atlantic coast emulating members from the Pacific coast in order to call the attention of the government to the miserable condition of the fishermen. Every session, from beginning to end, members from western Canada spend their energy defending the cause of the wheat producers who, having known a great prosperity, now find themselves in a difficult situation, although they get the lion's share in the distribution of the favours granted by this house.
A foreigner, having read our Hansard for a number of years, would be under the impression that wheat producing is our only major agricultural industry, and the only one having suffered in recent years.
As the number of hon. members who are interested in dairying is limited, we are apt to forget how that industry has developed in every province of Canada.
I wish to devote this, my first speech in this house, to the dairy industry which is the most important in my constituency and in my province, and which is seldom discussed in this house, but which is nevertheless

The Budget-Mr. Leclerc
the greatest and most important agricultural industry in Canada. In order to show its importance, sir, let me quote a few figures. Although prices have been abnormally low for a long time, the annual value of its products during the last six or seven years still averaged the imposing figure of 200 million odd dollars.
The progress of the dairy industry has been going on steadily in every province of Canada. The number of farmers interested in that industry is 318,000, and 50,000 persons are employed in allied industries. If we add together the heads of families and their dependents working in all branches of that industry, we find that they represent nearly 17 per cent of the total population of the country. This is a very large proportion, possibly the largest, employed in a single industry in Canada.
There has 'been no decrease in the number of workers in the dairy industry during the last few years of economic depression. This is conclusive proof that this industry is the most stable in Canada, even though it does not receive the full consideration it deserves.
Notwithstanding the increase in prices for farm products during the last two years, for butter and cheese particularly, bringing new hope to the farmers, one cannot overlook the serious trouble the latter experienced from 1931 to 1935, when butter dropped as low as 15 and 16 cents a pound, the lowest level reached in more than fifty years, so much so that in certain sections of the country it was used as a lubricant.
The government of the time did not even think of fixing a minimum price for this product, though they were doing it for wheat and other grain. It was no doubt because no representations were being made on behalf of the dairy industry that such discrimination took place where one class benefited at the expense of another.
Mr. Speaker, in spite of the improved prices for dairy products, the total income of an able farmer is no higher than the annual wage of any factory worker.
Here is a summary of the income that may be derived from a good farm in the eastern townships, a farm where 20 cows can be kept. On the basis of the prevailing prices for the. last two years, the average annual income from a cow is approximately $30, which means that the total income derived from the herd is only $600 a year. If we add to that another amount of $600 which a farmer can obtain from the sale of other farm products such as pork, beef, eggs, maple syrup, and so on, we have his gross income. Let us consider what the farmer has to pay for feed, fertilizer
and so on, and what he has to pay for municipal and school taxes, insurance, maintenance of farm buildings, interest, and for the purchase of new farm machinery, the cost of all this being entirely out of proportion with the price he obtains for his farm products. It can thus be seen, Mr. Speaker, that he cannot make both ends meet, and that his farm cannot be successfully operated.
Besides, we must not forget that, in order to earn such a small income, the farmer, as well as his wife and children, must toil from sunrise to sunset every day of the week, including Sunday, for the forty-hour week and minimum salaries are unknown on the farm.
In farming communities, needy farmers are dealt with by municipal authorities with less consideration than is given to city indigents. In this connection, I may mention the fact that a farmer was forced to sell his herd of ten milk cows in order to pay for the hospital care of a member of his family.
Mr. Speaker, the plight of farmers is one of the most serious social problems of our times. Therein lies the true reason why people give up farming, considering that all members of the community have a right to entertain common aspirations. Can country people be prevented from yearning after simple comforts, and from being dazzled by their friends from the city who display an artificial luxury which is often bought on instalments. Some of them can see no future for themselves or for their children in farming. Many young country people look for work in the cities, where they replace old men who will eventually have to be cared for by the State.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I overstated the plight of a great number of our farmers. In my opinion, it is useless to try to improve through ai'tificial means, the diets which prevail in towns, if we fail to create normal life conditions for the tillers of the soil. We would even be doing a service to city workmen in putting a stop to that unceasing migration of families and young people from rural districts, through which the number of those who compete with city workmen is constantly growing.
Mr. Speaker, I fully grasp the difficulties which governments must face. They cannot subsidize all industries without falling into the excesses of socialism. However, I have never heard any good reason for fixing a minimum price for wheat, or for subsidizing production of that cereal in preference to any other branch of agriculture. We have had a commission to regulate the price of wheat, we have a permanent tariff board to protect the legitimate interests of industry. All those
The Budget-Mr. Leclerc

commissions have undoubtedly been useful but. in the economic machinery of this country, there are other branches of the farming industry which need assistance, especially the dairy industry. Whenever minimum prices are again set for wheat, we must demand the same consideration for the dairy industry.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of this house a new problem which faces the dairy industry. I refer to the vegetable oils imported into Canada for the last few years, coconut, cottonseed, palm, and peanut oils. These oils are refined and made comestible; a large quantity is employed in the production of shortening, salad oils, etc. The inedible oils are used in the manufacture of soap, paint, varnish, lubricants, etc. It is obvious that shortening is displacing to a certain extent the natural lard of Canada even among the farming people. Statistics show that the production of lard is on the decrease ir. Canada on account of the fact that bacon pork does not give as much lard as the fat pork produced in the past. In the last few years we have heard a good deal of recrimination on account of the importation of vegetable oils. It is rather difficult to estimate exactly the harm done to the dairy industry by those importations because the statistics show that the consumption of butter for 1937 increased by 10,000,000 pounds over that of 1936, and by 100.000,000 pounds over that of 1925. This new problem must not be overlooked if we want to prevent the refined product of foreign countries, highly advertised by the large packing companies, to jeopardize the future of our dairy industry.
Mr. Speaker, one of the farmer's most serious problems is undoubtedly the disequilibrium between the prices of agricultural products and those of manufactured goods. Certainly, I am in favour of social laws ensuring reasonable wages and a reasonable standard of living to the factory worker. But, unfortunately, the farmer now feels the incidence of such laws, having no reasonable wage assured to him, nor a minimum price fixed for his products. Born on a farm, I am acquainted with the work and drudgery of a farmer's life. Having carried on dairy farming all my life, I am perhaps in a better position than others to know the difficulties and sacrifices which the farmers have had to undergo for several years past.
I pay respectful homage to the organizations of courageous farm women of my constituency and my province. They are to be admired for their helpful cooperation and the moral encouragement they are giving to agricultural undertakings. I should be sorry if I failed to mention the clubs of

young farmers of my constituency, for which I entertain great hopes. By their practical studies they are becoming, I am convinced, model farmers who will, in their respective centres, contribute to the spreading of the best methods of farming which will ensure the prosperity of our rural districts.
As to the advantages of cooperation, I take pleasure in quoting a few paragraphs of the collective pastoral letter of the bishops of the province of Quebec on the rural problem in relation to the social doctrine of the church and on the dangers which threaten our rural population.
Shall we first venture to state that rural life remains the normal condition of the masses? In a century when all kinds of attractions and needs have, in most countries, uprooted the rural populations to concentrate them in the cities, we should not, it would seem, seek to return to their fields so many improvised townsmen, nor even retain on the land those who are still there. Doubtless, and we readily admit it, rural life can no longer be conceived with the same remoteness and hardships which it formerly offered to the peasants who are entitled as much as anybody else to the benefits of modern science and invention. The fact nevertheless remains that, in spite of the development of manufacturing processes, the fundamental industry will always consist in draw-ing from the land the daily bread of mankind.
We could at this point paint a happy picture of rural life and describe all its advantages for the individual, the family and society. But, it must be admitted, this happpiness is not common; unless we succeed in placing rural economy on a more stable basis, it will probably vanish altogether. The products which the farmer offers for sale do not bring prices equal to those of the products of industry. And the economic recovery which is gradually manifesting itself in the wages paid to industrial workers is not so apparent in the domain of farming.
The years of depression, from the effects of which the rural districts are recovering more slowly than the cities, have brought about a general distaste for farm work-more particularly among the youth of the country who are more and more attracted by other occupations, seemingly more remunerative, in factories, mines and lumber camps. Tired of the daily complaints of their parents who have difficulty in making ends meet, these young men from the country seek elsewhere employment which they consider more remunerative.
Other causes, however, have accentuated this distaste. A more or less conscious opinion exists among most people that farming is an occupation to which one should resign oneself only as a last resort; that with a modicum of schooling, one should hasten to leave the plough, and that, in order to progress in life, one should settle in the village at least, if not in the city, however lowly the work to be found there. On the other hand, many city people, especially among those whose prosperity is of recent date, are fond of displaying in the village of their birth a sham and superficial luxury and using patronizing airs towards the intimidated countryman.

The Budget-Mr. Tremblay
Cooperative societies protect their members against their own temptations and against the unfair competition of others. Therefore, one of the most pressing things to teach to the farmer is the pecuniary profit he will derive, in addition to peace of conscience, from cooperating with his fellow-farmers instead of working in an underhand way. In fact, the isolated family is exposed to routine methods of farming and is unable to defend itself easily against costly middlemen in the purchase of farm implements and other requirements.
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to bring my full support to these wise teachings.
It was established during the inquiry on the prices of farm implements that the marketing and distribution of farm implements increase the selling price to the farmers by 25 to 40 per cent. Then why not buy and sell through cooperative organizations? Such organizations would have not hundreds, but thousands of members. I am convinced that they would tend greatly to eliminate the middleman in the selling of farm products and the buying of farm implements.
Mr. Speaker, I was glad to hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) say that he is establishing machinery for better advertising of our farm products in the United Kingdom. I personally, noticed that New Zealand keeps its products well to the fore in the London markets. In fact, what strikes you most in London is the words "New Zealand butter- New Zealand cheese-" in large letters on the busses.
Therefore, I congratulate the Minister of Agriculture for his publicity campaign in regard to our products. I urge the house to give serious consideration to my remarks. To bring prosperity back to agriculture is to give their purchasing power back to the farmers, and it is the safest way to solve Canada's economic and agricultural problem.
Mr. Speaker, before concluding may I quote the following words from Honore Mercier:
Agriculture, specially in the province of Quebec, is at the basis of public prosperity. Rivers and streams could be turned from their course, artificial works could, for a time, give satisfactory results, but it would be foolish to rely for the future on any other basis than that which agriculture offers us.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to take part in this debate, but inspiration came to me this afternoon while listening to my hon. friend from Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Lapointe). I congratulate him warmly for having raised certain matters worthy of consideration and for having pointed out certain anomalies, to say the least, in the administration of the Canadian National Railways. These anomalies will no doubt be attended to by the minister of Transport (Mr. Howe). I took note of the
statement of my hon. friend from Matapedia-Matane. I do not know if I have his exact words, but here it is as I took it:
It is a rather extraordinary thing that the stations situated between La Reine and Fitzpatrick and between Noranda and Taschereau, covering a distance of 411 miles, all in Quebec province, are under the jurisdiction of an Ontario superintendent.
The hon. member also pointed out this other anomaly:
The same situation exists on the Gaspd Coast and from Matapedia to Riviere du Loup, a stretch of 366 miles, where a New Brunswick superintendent is in charge.
I do not know if that is evidence of bad faith. Such a situation would at least call for an explanation. As to freight cars going from Lake St. John to the neighbouring province or, worse still, to Western Canada, for repairs, whereas such work could be done in the province of Quebec, it seems to me that we have grounds for complaint, and I say once again that my hon. friend from Matapedia-Matane deserves congratulations for having called the attention of the house to those matters.
My hon. friend also spoke against the amalgamation of our two railways, and he has my complete approval.
He certainly voiced public sentiment in the Province of Quebec when he stated that we opposed amalgamation of the two Canadian systems.
I have carefully read the evidence given in this connection by Mr. Hungerford and I believe that we must inevitably come to the same conclusion after considering the reasons he offers against an amalgamation of the two railways. Prospects of substantial economies through the unification of our two railways were dangled before our eyes, but the evidence given by Mr. Hungerford shows, I believe, that this is but a bait. With your permission, I would like to quote a few extracts from the report. He states, for instance:
To sum up my position with regard to the asserted economies from unification or amalgamation, it is my judgment that they are largely unrealizable. Railway savings purchased at the expense of the development of Canada and of a wide disturbance in the already disturbed labour and material markets of the country would be too dearly obtained. The country instead of being better off would be worse off. Yet it is only to the extent that a program of drastic reduction in expenses could be achieved that the country would be warranted in inviting the perils of monopoly and of the great difficulties which I foresee in the type of management of the joint enterprise which is now proposed.
And a little farther on in the report, Mr. Hungerford states that savings could be realized' through cooperation, willingly given
The Budget-Mr. Tremblay

or enforced, and his suggestions, as I see them, are practical ones. He suggests, among other things:
Most of the economies which are realizable in a practical sense, in that they relate to economies which can really be made effective without unduly impairing the public interest, will be found upon examination to be obtainable under the principle of cooperation and the country need not incur all of the unknown perils of unification in order to obtain these economies.
I am satisfied that he is perfectly correct. Of course, if one takes a different viewpoint, if those who favour a monopoly of railways in this country give consideration only to eventual profits or dividends, I can readily understand their zeal in promoting unification of the two railway systems. But as far as we are concerned, representing as we do the interests of the people and intending to fulfill our duty, we are overwhelmingly opposed to unification.
A distinguished newspaperman from Quebec city, who does not always share our views, but who holds good ones often enough, Mr. Eugene L'Heureux, of L'Action Catho-lique, made the following statement in an editorial dated June 17:
The Hungerford plan seems to us sounder, broader and in closer harmony with the real interests of Canada than the other.
The other is the plan put forward by the promoters of unification or, in other words, of monopoly.
We would be mistaken in taking the view that this railway problem is merely a budget matter. The railways are not built for their own benefit, but for that of the nation. Such is the reason why we cannot properly appreciate their financial statement save in the light of their contribution not only to the economic but also to the general progress of the country. If we must shoulder a twenty-five million annual railway deficit, still if they make the development of the country possible as well as that of every section of it, then we may find compensation for it many times over.
In the new settlements, for instance, the railways generally do not earn enough to cover their operating expenses. But shall it be said that just because the railways have a deficit in those settlements, settlers and new settlements must be deprived of the advantages of a railway? Such is not my opinion. That is a viewpoint which the promoters of amalgamation do not take into account at all, but which we must remember nevertheless.
There is another point raised by Mr. Hungerford in his report, and we understand better why the Canadian National Railways have been suffering such large deficits. Let us take the period from 1927 to 1930. Mr. Hungerford has this to say about that period: 
The Canadian National Railways, from the onset of the depression in the fall of 1929 until the middle of 1930, pursued a policy of maintaining at work on the property all its staff for which legitimate employment could be found, rather than taking the drastic step of wholesale dismissals, closing down of shops, etc. This policy, whether well-founded or not, was publicly announced and supported in parliament.
And I say that parliament was perfectly justified in doing so and that it was simply discharging its duty. As regards this railway problem, the possible income or profits of the railway at the end of the year is not the only thing to be considered. Had we considered the question otherwise, what real economies could we have realized? Thousands of men would have been added to those already unemployed, and this house would have been called upon to vote large sums of money to assist those discharged by the Canadian National Railways.
That is the reason why I am definitely opposed to unification or monopoly. I would leave it to Mr. Hungerford whose statement was commented upon by a Quebec newspaper. He says:
I maintain that monopoly is no inducement to good management. I believe it involves a risk of demoralization in the business, a loss of initiative and enthusiasm, a lack of sympathetic understanding between the officers and the staff, between the management and the public.
Moreover, I am not in favour of a railway monopoly in Canada. I sincerely believe that it would be highly detrimental to the public and that it would be contrary to the course we intended to follow when we established the Canadian railways, which aimed at developing new districts impossible of access until those lines were built up.
I will not labour the point but I wanted to say to the house that any scheme of unification or monopolization is one that should be seriously examined.
I come to the conclusion, as Mr. Hungerford states, that if we were to set up a commission composed of a representative of the Canadian National Railways, a representative of the Canadian Pacific Railway and a representative of the government cooperating with a view to improving services in the various parts of the country and to eliminating duplication in some others, we could effect large savings without any prejudice to the people of Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is another question on which I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe). I have here the official report of the Royal Commission on Anthracite Coal and I read it from beginning to end. For some time now I have requested the National Harbours

The Budget-Mr. McKinnon
Board to try to utilize the space called " public wharf " in the Quebec harbour. Last year, a certain space was put at the disposal of the public for coal importations but, as it was a public place to which anyone had access, it was clear that the period of time in which it could be used was limited. The National Harbours Board issued a regulation dealing with the use of this public wharf and it was no surprise to me that they set a time limit of three weeks in case others might claim the same privileges. I brought to the attention of the National Harbours Board the fact that the regulation under which that public wharf could be used during that period would freeze-out all possible competitors of the coal monopoly in Quebec. Thus was removed in Quebec all serious competition against the trust of the Webster group which is described as such by the Tory report. Limiting to three weeks the period of time during which a coal importer could use this public wharf would have the effect of eliminating all competition.
The Minister of Transport had to answer a few questions I asked him about the use of that public wharf. I had anticipated the situation and I hope that action will be taken with a view to remedying it. The National Harbours Board has already received communications wherein the request is made that responsible organizations, financially sound, be permitted to organize for the importation of coal, which they are not allowed to do at the present time. For instance, who would care, with this regulation allowing the wharf to be used for three weeks only, to incur the cost of setting up machinery for unloading and handling coal? They have to use the machinery of their competitors, the powerful Webster concern operating under the name of St. Lawrence Stevedoring Company.
The commissioner appointed by the honourable the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) had this to say about the St. Lawrence Stevedoring Company, as shown on page 79 of his report:
Your commission believes it ie justified in calling special attention to the profits of the St. Lawrence Stevedoring Company. This company has practically no commercial risks; it does not buy or sell coal; it merely unloads, prepares and delivers coal for the companies of the Webster group and, in addition, unloads or tranships coal and small quantities of other commodities for other occasional customers.
And I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to take notice of the following statement made by the Commissioner :
The St. Lawrence Stevedoring Company has outstanding $200,000 of fully paid capital stock; its permanent assets are valued at $146,000; its accounts receivable (due almost entirely from the British Coal Corporation) -
As every one knows, that means again the Webster group.
-are $470,000, its cash on hand $60,000. In the three years 1933, 1934 and 1935, its net profits were $360,000, $391,000 and $250,000; a total of over $1,000,000, or an average of 167 per cent per annum on its paid-up capital stock. In other words, the rates it charges its own associated companies are grossly out of proportion to its cost of operation and the responsibility it assumes.
To that company the Webster group's competitors will have to apply as regards the handling of the coal imported by them. Should they ever dare to compete with that all powerful group, I feel sure that, under such unfavourable conditions, they would not remain long in business.
I wished to bring these matters to the attention of the house. Knowing as I do the ability and patriotism of the Minister of Transport, whom I greatly esteem and trust, I am convinced that he will give to my remarks his most sympathetic consideration. I wish to thank him in advance and I hope that before long we, in Quebec, will be afforded an opportunity of witnessing genuine competition in the importation of fuel.
I could quote another paragraph from Mr. Tory's report,-paragraph 21, on page 117:
Retailers' gross margins have also generally declined since 1930. In the city of Ottawa, however, the retailers' margins are much higher than in Quebec, Montreal or Toronto. In Quebec city, where the Canadian Import Company has a complete monopoly of the wholesale trade, the wholesale price is $1 higher than in Montreal, while the margin for the retail dealer is exceedingly narrow.
The report of this royal commission should be read by every one. It should be circulated, in order that the public may be made aware of the methods used by their exploiters. The word is not too strong. Every page of this report reveals the coal trust's desire constantly to extend its tentacles and to make exorbitant profits. I ask the minister to take the measures required to give Quebec the benefit of competition in the matter of fuel.
I wish to add a word of appreciation of the general policies enunciated in the budget speech. The general situation is extremely encouraging and we have reason not only to feel proud of the present government, but also to view the future with the greatest optimism.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon the financial showing for the fiscal year 1937-38, the deficit of $13,775,000 being substantially less than the minister had thought it safe to predict a year ago, and also sub-

The Budget-Mr. McKinnon
stantially less than when we headed into the . deipression eight years ago. The remarkable thing about this financial showing is that it comes at a period when world economic conditions are receding and also at a time when Canada has been hard hit through having a series of droughts in the western wheat fields.
As the member for Kenora-Rainy River, which district is the bottle-neck through which western grain moving to the east must pass, I am much gratified over the present prospect of a western crop this year. With both transcontinental rail lines passing through the riding, the railroad industry is of great importance to the district. The people of the district will rejoice with the farmers of the west over crop prospects for three reasons: First, as a relief to the farmers themselves after a series of heart-breaking experiences; second, 'because of the general improvement that will follow throughout Canada from a more prosperous west and, third, because of the improvement in the railroad industry and what this will mean to the employees.
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance drew a sharp distinction between pump priming and government assistance to the building construction industry, where such assistance is aimed at stimulating private endeavour. This distinction is a most proper one. The steps which the government is proposing to parliament in the form of advancing money for municipal works construction, the broadening of the scheme of loans for private housing construction and greater assistance to low rental housing schemes are all in the proper direction. I would suggest that dominion participation in these schemes be such that in addition to careful administration of the dominion end of these projects the operation of the various acts be thoroughly and constantly watched and studied so that each year the federal government may be advised what further steps should be taken, what additional measures should be applied and what changes should be made in order that parliament may 'be asked to pass such further legislation or amendments to existing legislation as are needed better to stimulate construction.
Though admittedly the volume of employment is better throughout Canada than a year ago, and considerably better than two or three years ago, it so happens that Kenora-Rainy River is one of the few ridings in which conditions are not as good as they were last year. It would seem that this riding is affected by the condition of every one of the industries which have experienced recessions as compared with a year ago. Because of

the western crop situation, railroading and flour milling in the district are depressed. Conditions in the United States have had an adverse effect upon the lumbering and pulp and paper industries. There are no opportunities for alternative employment in northwestern Ontario such as exist in other districts. This district has only a few industries, and in bad times it must rely on governmental assistance, though of course in good times this is not the case.
With reference to the general subject of employment, may I say I feel that such a step as the creation of the national employment commission was a move in the right direction. My only criticism is that there should be such a body, possibly in a different form, more or less permanent in character in order constantly to study Canada's employment needs and problems. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) promised the appointment of a committee to carry on some of the work begun by the national employment commission. I express the hope that this matter will receive early attention and that the government will set up some competent board of permanent advisers to consider the all-important matter of employment.
I heartily approve the policy of the government in continuing the Canadian National Railways as a separate enterprise. It is quite true that the railway deficit is serious, but that is the price we must pay for the undue optimism of years ago in connection with railways and also because of our great distances. This deficit, which should be reduced when conditions warrant, would have to be paid in some form or another by the people of Canada regardless of what shift there may occur in the management of the railways.
The budget contains an exemption from income tax of lump sum payments into pension schemes by employers. This is a step in the right direction. Employers and employees should receive every encouragement to build up pension funds for the protection of the employees, along similar lines to the civil service pension fund. In this way employees will be taken care of in old age, they will be able to maintain their selfrespect and they will not become- public charges. The government might very well watch this pension scheme business in order to discover whether there is not some other way in which employers and employees can be encouraged to enter into such scheme.
As with pensions, so with the lifting of the sales tax on building materials. This should be quite a help to the workers through giving assistance to the building industry. I

Questions
suggest a constant study of building and construction in order to devise ways and means of aiding that basic industry. This principle of easy taxes to encourage building should receive particular attention.
If the experience of the last several years has taught us anything, it has taught us the need of unemployment insurance. Prolonged unemployment and heavy relief costs without a dollar saved to meet the situation at its beginning should prove the need of some such provision as unemployment insurance if we are going to care properly for our population. I realize that the scope of the dominion is limited in this field, but the scheme should be national in order to be effective. I hope the dominion government will pursue to a conclusion the present policy of seeking provincial agreement to a dominion scheme. In no event should the utmost necessity be lost from sight. Should the negotiations with the provinces not yield a final conclusion within a reasonable time, then the dominion government should canvass the situation thoroughly in order to discover what alternative course might be adopted by the parliament of Canada to ensure a national scheme. As a first step toward unemployment insurance the dominion government might see what could be done about taking over the public employment offices. These would be needed for the insurance scheme, and in any event any scheme to grapple with employment would require a good system of employment exchanges under the sole control of the dominion.
I feel that if a few of these schemes were put into effect, they would go a long way toward taking care of the situation that will no doubt arise in the future. If we build up a sound unemployment scheme, I am sure that when the next depression strikes us we shall not find ourselves in the same difficulty as that in which we have been during the last eight years. I hope the government may see its way clear during this session of parliament to implement some of the recommendations I have made.
On motion of Mr. Marsh the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the house adjourned at 10.57 p.m.
Thursday, June 23, 1938
